articles.title: What Is Oud? A Beginner’s Guide to Oud Fragrance
articles.summary: Understand oud, read a fragrance description with confidence and find a starting point for your first sample.
articles.body:
Oud is an aromatic material associated with agarwood: resin-rich wood from trees including Aquilaria and Gyrinops. In fragrance shopping, “oud” can also describe a scent direction within a blended perfume. Understanding that distinction makes it easier to choose a fragrance without assuming every oud product smells alike.

Agarwood, oud oil and oud perfume

Agarwood refers to the resinous wood. Oud oil is a material obtained from agarwood, while an oud perfume is a finished fragrance composition. A perfume may combine an oud impression with other notes. Its name alone does not establish its ingredient source or formula.

When you browse a collection, look for the product’s actual ingredient information and the scent description. Treat a note list as guidance about the fragrance experience rather than a certificate of origin. Claims about a specific wood, region or concentration should come from the individual product’s verified information.

What does oud smell like?

You may encounter descriptions such as woody, smoky, resinous or sweet. These words are useful starting points, but a finished perfume is a combination. A fruit-led fragrance with an oud note can feel different from one presented around woods and incense. “Oud” is too broad a label to make the whole decision for you.

Read the surrounding notes. Do you already enjoy citrus, soft musk, fruit or a richer woody direction? Starting with a familiar preference can make exploring a new fragrance category less overwhelming.

How to choose your first oud fragrance

  1. Choose one familiar note. Search the OUDIE scent explorer for a name or note you already enjoy.
  2. Read the whole description. Notice the other notes alongside oud, rather than choosing by a single word.
  3. Compare the format. A perfume and an oil are different ways to wear a scent. Check the intended use on the product page.
  4. Start with a sample where available. Spend time with the fragrance before committing to a full-size format.

Keep scent and format separate

Your scent choice answers what you want to smell. Your format choice answers how you want to use it. On OUDIE scent cards, the available-format choices let you explore the same scent across matching products. Availability varies by scent, so confirm the selection and price on the product page.

A car diffuser or room-oriented product should not be treated as a skin fragrance. Always follow the instructions for the product you choose.

Where to start with OUDIE

Explore scents by name or note, or browse fragrance samples. If you prefer to begin with a format, visit perfumes or oil blends. You do not need to choose the most intense-sounding description to enjoy exploring oud.

Further reading

For the botanical distinction, see Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: CITES and Timber, the agarwood section. This reference explains the material; it does not verify the ingredients of any individual OUDIE product.

articles.title: Perfume Oil vs Extrait de Parfum: How to Choose Your Format
articles.summary: Compare oil and spray formats by the way you prefer to apply fragrance, then check the exact scent and product details.
articles.body:
Choose perfume oil or extrait de parfum by considering the application you prefer and the details of the particular product. A format name alone does not tell you exactly how long a scent will last or how it will feel on you.

Start with the scent you want

If you already love a fragrance, start there. Check which formats are offered for that scent, then compare their product pages. You may have fewer choices for one scent than another; the available-format controls should show actual matching products.

At OUDIE, the same scent identity can appear in more than one product format. That lets you explore another way to use a familiar scent. It does not mean that every product has an identical formula, size, price or intended use.

Think about your application routine

A spray format and an oil format ask for different application habits. Check the packaging and instructions of the exact item you plan to buy. Consider whether you prefer a spray bottle at home or an oil application as part of your routine.

Neither choice needs a universal “better” label. The useful question is whether the product suits how you plan to wear fragrance. Follow its directions rather than applying a rule from an unrelated perfume.

Compare the information that matters

QuestionWhat to check
Is this my scent?The selected scent name and variant on the product page.
How do I use it?Product instructions and intended application.
What am I buying?Format, size, current price and availability.
What is in it?Verified ingredient information for that product.
Can I try it first?The available sample options and their contents.

Avoid choosing by a longevity promise alone

Do not assume that “oil” or “extrait” guarantees a fixed number of hours. A broad format label cannot replace the information about a particular composition. If wear is your main concern, ask about the item and try a sample where possible.

Notice whether you enjoy the fragrance after the opening impression as well as when you first encounter it. Choosing something you want to return to is more useful than comparing a number with no context.

Keep home and car formats in their own lane

A scent may also be available in a mist, car diffuser or car freshener. These are separate products. Check their intended use; do not assume that a familiar scent name makes every format suitable for skin.

Choose a format with OUDIE

Browse oil blends if that is your preferred starting point, or explore extrait de parfum. On a scent card, select a format to see its matching price and purchase destination. The product page gives you the final selection before adding to your bag.

Still deciding on the scent itself? Visit Explore Scents or check sample options before choosing a full-size product.

articles.title: Understanding Fragrance Notes: How to Choose Oud and Musk Scents
articles.summary: Use top, heart and base notes as a starting point for discovery, then compare the fragrance as a whole.
articles.body:
Top, heart and base notes are a way to describe a fragrance’s unfolding impression. Use them to discover a direction you like, then consider the whole composition. A note list is a starting point for comparison, not a promise that every person will experience the scent in exactly the same way.

What are top, heart and base notes?

Top notes describe the opening impression. Heart notes describe the central character as that opening develops. Base notes describe the foundation of the fragrance. The layers give you a vocabulary for talking about what you notice over time.

These labels are useful without a stopwatch. You do not need to assign an exact minute to every change in order to enjoy a fragrance. Let the composition develop and notice which parts appeal to you.

Choose a note you already recognise

Think about fragrances you have enjoyed before. Was it the citrus opening, a fruit note, a floral character or a musky foundation? Search by that preference rather than trying to interpret every name in a long note list.

A single familiar note can lead to several different scents. Compare the other listed notes and leave room for the fragrance to surprise you. Two compositions mentioning musk can still offer different overall experiences.

Read OUDIE examples in context

OUDIE Madawi lists peach, apple blossom and pineapple blossom alongside oud. OUDIE Musk lists citrus, bergamot, white musk and aloe vera. These are examples of the scent information in OUDIE’s catalogue, rather than claims about raw ingredient sourcing.

Use the scent explorer to compare the current descriptions. Search “peach” if fruit is your starting point, or “musk” if you want to explore that direction. Check the full product page before buying, since the format and selected variant still matter.

A note list is not an ingredient declaration

Fragrance descriptions and product ingredient information have different jobs. A scent note helps describe the smell. For questions about the actual formula, consult the product’s ingredient information or ask the team about the exact item.

Likewise, a scent name does not confirm a botanical origin, concentration or sourcing practice. Avoid reading those assumptions into an evocative description.

A simple way to compare samples

  1. Choose a small shortlist with one familiar note in common.
  2. Follow each product’s directions for use.
  3. Write down your first impression in plain words.
  4. Return to the fragrance later and note what you still enjoy.
  5. Compare your notes before choosing a full-size format.

You do not need expert vocabulary. “I like the fruit at the start” or “I prefer the softer impression later” is useful information.

Continue your discovery

Explore samples, then return to your chosen scent and select an available format. If you would like a guided group experience, learn about OUDIE fragrance workshops and bars.

Further reading

The International Perfume Museum’s guide to olfactory composition illustrates the top, heart and base framework. OUDIE examples above come from our own scent catalogue.

articles.title: Wedding Fragrance Bars in Toronto: What to Ask Before Booking
articles.summary: Plan a wedding fragrance experience with useful questions about guest flow, venue needs, scent selection and the proposal.
articles.body:
A wedding fragrance bar gives guests a guided way to discover scents during your celebration. Before booking one in Toronto, Mississauga or the GTA, ask how the experience will fit your venue, reception schedule and guest count. Clear details make it easier to assess a proposal.

1. What will guests actually do?

Ask the provider to describe the guest journey from arrival to finish. Will guests explore a curated selection, receive recommendations or take part in a hands-on activity? A fragrance bar and a blending workshop are different formats, so clarify which one you are discussing.

OUDIE offers guided fragrance bars and separate private workshops. Start with the experience you want guests to have, then discuss how it can fit your wedding.

2. When will the bar be part of the celebration?

Consider the welcome period, reception transitions and the evening schedule. Share your planned timing with the provider and your planner. Ask how arrivals will be handled and whether the proposal suits the way guests will move through the event.

Do not assume that an activity can run for the entire reception. Confirm the service window and any setup or pack-down arrangements in writing.

3. What does the venue need to provide?

Ask about the footprint, table requirements, access and setup location. Your venue coordinator can help review the space and any restrictions. If fragrance will be used indoors, discuss the placement thoughtfully alongside dining, flowers and the other parts of your celebration.

Share the venue name as soon as it is available. If you are still choosing, provide the city and the type of setting so the first conversation can begin.

4. How is the scent selection chosen?

Tell the provider what you and your partner enjoy. Ask how a menu is curated and whether there are presentation options to discuss. You can explore OUDIE’s scent catalogue beforehand, while keeping in mind that an event’s selection is agreed separately.

You do not need to pick every scent before making an inquiry. A short description of the atmosphere you want is a helpful starting point.

5. What is included in the proposal?

Confirm staffing, materials, any guest takeaway, presentation and the service window. If bottles or personalisation are part of your request, ask what is possible and how those details affect the proposal. Do not assume a specific bottle size, quantity or inclusion until it is confirmed.

Ask about the process for changes to attendance, travel arrangements and booking terms. A useful proposal should let you understand the scope as well as the price.

6. What should you send in the first inquiry?

  • Your names and contact email.
  • The wedding date, or an approximate period if undecided.
  • The city and venue if known.
  • An approximate guest count.
  • The fragrance experience you have in mind.
  • Questions about timing, presentation or inclusions.

Plan an OUDIE experience

OUDIE is based in Mississauga and welcomes inquiries for Toronto and the GTA. For another location, include it in your message so availability and travel can be discussed.

Tell us about your wedding through the Experiences inquiry form. Sending an inquiry begins the conversation; it does not confirm a booking.
